# Preface {.unnumbered}

This is the book form of **ECON 8310: Business Forecasting** at the University of Nebraska at
Omaha. It is not a summary of the course and not a replacement for it — it is the same material in
a format you can read, search and quote from.

Every chapter is one lecture, and carries that lecture's title exactly. Within a chapter, each
section is a slide from the deck: the table, figure or definition the class saw, followed by what
was said about it.

## How this book is made

Nothing here is written twice. Each chapter is **generated** from the course's own files — the
Quarto mirror of the Beamer deck, and the recording script written for that lecture — by
`scripts/build_book.py`. The consequence matters more than the mechanism: a number, a table or a
figure in this book cannot disagree with the deck it came from, because it is never copied. It is
read from the deck on every build.

That property is not decoration. Over one week in August 2026 the course found three reported
figures that no committed code reproduced, a diagnostics table whose headline claim the
reproducible numbers contradicted, and a tuning result that was noise. Each had been correct when
written and had quietly stopped being so. A book assembled by hand would have inherited all of
them.

## What the course is about

One dataset, measured honestly, method after method.

Every model in this book is fitted to the same panel of thirty Walmart store-category series and
scored on the same held-out block, so the numbers can be put beside one another. The result is not
the one anyone predicts in week one: a 46-coefficient linear model finishes at the top, ahead of
four neural architectures, and the two with the most attention behind them finish fifth and sixth.

The chapters explain why, from the data rather than from the reputation of the methods. That is
the actual subject: not which model wins, but how to find out, and how to tell when a confident
number has not earned its confidence.
